posts.title: The three great teachers
posts.caption:
Who actually wrote Ayurveda down? 🌿

Three texts are known together as the Brihat Trayi, the great triad: the Charaka Samhita, the Sushruta Samhita and the Ashtanga Hridaya.

One is the text of internal medicine. One is the surgical text. The third gathers both into an ordered handbook that students could memorise, and it is still taught today.

Their dates? Scholars date the Charaka text between the 4th century BCE and the 2nd century CE, with a later revision about the 6th century CE, and they say plainly that the dates are uncertain.

The posts on either side of this reel open each text and say what is inside.

posts.title: What people claim, and what is written
posts.caption:
Five things people say about Sushruta, checked against the sources. 🌿

Part 3 of tonight's posts. Swipe through:

1. Did the text describe nose surgery? Supported.
2. Was he the world's first surgeon? Not supported by anything we can cite.
3. Did one man write the whole book? No. It took shape over centuries.
4. Where does the teaching come from? Tradition says Dhanvantari; earlier manuscripts say Divodasa.
5. Do we have his original manuscript? No. The oldest copy is from 878 CE.

Respect means checking, not inflating. The record is remarkable enough on its own.

alt: Cover: Myth and record. What people claim about Sushruta, and what is written. Five claims checked against the sources, above a low horizon line with sprigs.
Claim one: Sushruta described rhinoplasty. Supported. Britannica confirms the text's surgical scope includes rhinoplasty.
Claim two: Sushruta was the first surgeon in history. Not supported. No citable source establishes a first.
Claim three: Sushruta wrote the whole book himself. Not supported. The text took shape over centuries and later hands revised it.
Claim four: the teaching came from Dhanvantari. Tradition. Later editions credit Dhanvantari; earlier manuscripts credit Divodasa, a king of Varanasi.
Claim five: we still have Sushruta's own manuscript. Not supported. The oldest surviving copy was completed on 13 April 878 CE, in Kathmandu.

These are not chemical elements. Classical Ayurveda describes the world, and the body within it, as a combination of five elements which are qualities and tendencies.
Three families of quality: space and air suggest lightness and movement, fire suggests heat and transformation, water and earth suggest cohesion and weight.

One language for body, food and season, because the elements describe qualities rather than substances.

Not a personality quiz. A dosha assessment is part of a clinical examination, done by a person, in front of you.

What a consultation covers: the complaint and its history, diet, appetite, digestion, sleep, daily habits, Prakriti and Vikriti, season, place, age, and a physical examination including pulse and tongue.

posts.title: Three doshas
posts.caption:
Everyone has all three. 🌿

The five elements combine into three functional principles, the doshas:

Vata, space and air, linked with movement.
Pitta, fire and water, linked with transformation and digestion.
Kapha, water and earth, linked with structure and lubrication.

Health is described as a state in which the doshas are balanced, and illness as their imbalance. There is no good dosha and no bad dosha. There is only proportion.

Which means you are not "a Vata". You carry all three, in your own proportion, and a practitioner reads that alongside your history, season and examination.

posts.title: Vata in motion
posts.caption:
Vata is not a personality type. 🌿

It is one of the three doshas: the pairing of space and air, traditionally linked with movement. In the body that reading covers breath, circulation, the passage of food, and the movement of thought.

The classical rule for working with it is simple: like increases like, opposites balance. So what is light, cold and erratic is met with what is warm, steady and grounded.

You carry all three doshas, in your own proportion. Being told you "are a Vata" is a shorthand, and a poor one.

This is general education, not a prescription. Assessment belongs to a practitioner who can examine you.

posts.title: Pitta at work
posts.caption:
Pitta is not a temper. 🌿

It is the pairing of fire and water, traditionally linked with transformation and digestion: turning food into the body, and impressions into understanding.

Digestion is not a side note in Ayurveda. The classical definition of a healthy person names it directly: doshas in equilibrium, digestion balanced, tissues in equilibrium, wastes eliminated properly, and the mind, senses and soul pleasant.

Which is why a consultation about temper asks about your meals and your sleep.

The working rule stays the same: opposites balance. Cool, steady, unhurried.

Roughly an hour and a half before sunrise. A muhurta is a traditional unit of about 48 minutes. Brahma Muhurta is usually reckoned as the one before the last of the night, so it moves with the sunrise and the season. So In Practice: It is tied to the sun, not to a clock time.

The day starts with its anchor. Everything in the daily routine hangs off waking time: the morning habits, the meals, the evening. A steady, early start is how the rest of the routine gets its rhythm.

Quiet, and unhurried. Many traditions use the hour for study, prayer or simply stillness before the household wakes. That use is widely taught, and it is a reasonable reading of why the hour is praised.

Not a productivity hack. We will not tell you that waking at four will change your metabolism or your career. The verse describes a routine for a healthy person. Anything beyond that is somebody else's claim.

Education, not dentistry. Bleeding gums, tooth pain and bad breath that will not go away have causes a dentist can find. A habit, old or new, is not a substitute for that examination.

A morning habit from the texts. Holding oil in the mouth appears in the classical daily routine, after cleaning the teeth and scraping the tongue. Oil pulling, as it is sold online, is a modern name for an old habit.
Hold, or swish: Gandusha, fill the mouth and hold, without moving; Kavala, a smaller amount, moved around the mouth.
Oil is one option. The texts describe several liquids for the mouth, chosen by purpose. Sesame oil is the one most people mean today. sesame oil, medicated oils, milk, decoctions, warm water.

One of eight signs. The eightfold examination reads the tongue alongside the pulse, voice, skin, eyes, stool, urine and general appearance. A vaidya may ask you not to scrape it on the morning of a visit.

One sign is not a finding. A coated or coloured tongue can follow food, drink, smoking, medicine or illness. On its own it tells you very little, which is why the examination reads eight signs together.

Easy on a sore mouth. Skip it if your tongue is sore, cut or ulcerated, and do not use it on young children. A strong gag reflex is a reason to keep it short and near the front.
Education, not dentistry. Persistent bad breath, a changing tongue or a painful mouth have causes a dentist or doctor can find. A habit is a habit. It does not replace that examination.

alt: Cover: Scraping the tongue. Jihwa nirlekhana: a two minute habit from the texts.

Jihwa, tongue. Nirlekhana, scraping.. The classical morning routine includes cleaning the tongue with a curved scraper after cleaning the teeth. It is one of the shortest habits in the whole routine. In One Line: Teeth first, then the tongue, then oil in the mouth.
Smooth, curved, blunt. The texts describe a smooth, curved scraper, traditionally of metal. What matters in practice is that the edge is blunt. copper, silver, steel, a smooth curve, a blunt edge.

Back to front, gently, a few times. Place the scraper towards the back of the tongue, draw it forward with light pressure, rinse, and repeat a few times. It should never hurt, and it should never draw blood.
Clean the whole mouth. The texts treat the mouth as a whole: teeth, tongue and gums each get a step. Scraping the tongue is simply the step that looks after the part a toothbrush tends to miss.

Not a detox for the body. We will not claim that scraping the tongue removes toxins from the body, improves digestion or cures anything. It is a hygiene habit described in the texts, and that is how we describe it.

Food, sleep and restraint. The Charaka Samhita names three upastambhas, supports of life: ahara, food; nidra, sleep; and brahmacharya, a disciplined, restrained life. Sleep sits beside food, not below it. Trayopastambha: The three sub pillars that hold up a healthy life.

Night sleep, mostly at night. The texts generally discourage daytime sleep for most people, with exceptions such as the hottest season, the very young, the old and the unwell. The rule is sleep when it is dark.

Early rising needs early sleep. Wednesday's early morning only works inside a routine that also sleeps early. Cutting sleep to rise sooner is not what the texts describe. They describe both ends of the night, together.
Not a sleep remedy. This is how a traditional system frames sleep. It is not a treatment for insomnia, and no herb on social media is a safe replacement for a conversation with a doctor.

Classical, or taught today?. Much of what is shared as Ayurvedic meal timing is modern teaching built on classical ideas. Both can be useful. They are still different statements, and we label them separately.
Which is which: Classical, eat after the last meal digests; Classical, eat in proper quantity; Taught today, largest meal around midday; Taught today, an early, light dinner.

The sun, and digestion. The popular reasoning is that digestion is described as strongest around midday, when the sun is highest. It is a reasonable reading of the tradition. It is not a verse we can cite.

Light, and not late. Most teaching agrees the last meal should be lighter and early enough to digest before sleep. That links meal timing straight back to Sunday's post on sleep. The Pattern: Supper that has digested by bedtime.

Eat when the last meal has digested. The Charaka Samhita's rules of eating include eating only after the previous meal has been digested. The clock is secondary. The real timer is digestion. Jirne Ashniyat: Eat after the previous meal is digested.

The signs of an empty stomach. Traditional teaching describes the signs: genuine hunger, a light body, a clear belch, easy bowels and a willingness to eat. Snacking before those arrive stacks one meal on another.
Back to Agni. The classical view treats weak or irregular digestion as a root of many disorders. Eating on top of an undigested meal is the most ordinary way to make digestion irregular.
Same times, most days. Once meals follow digestion, they tend to settle into steady times. That regularity is the part our guide puts first: regular meals, regular sleep, eating with the season.
Not a weight loss plan. Meal timing in the texts is about digestion and routine. We will not sell it as a diet, and anyone with diabetes or on medicine should plan meal times with their doctor.

Three doshas, three sets: Vata, sweet, sour, salty; Pitta, sweet, bitter, astringent; Kapha, pungent, bitter, astringent.

alt: Cover: Six tastes, not four. Shadrasa: how Ayurveda sorts every flavour.

Rasa means taste. The classical texts name six tastes and use them to describe every food and medicine. Taste is not only pleasure here. It is the first way a substance is classified. Shad Rasa: Shad, six. Rasa, taste.
Sweet, sour, salty: Madhura, sweet: rice, milk, ghee; Amla, sour: lemon, curd, tamarind; Lavana, salty: rock salt, sea salt.
Pungent, bitter, astringent: Katu, pungent: ginger, pepper, chilli; Tikta, bitter: neem, bitter gourd; Kashaya, astringent: pulses, unripe banana.

Each taste has two elements. The texts describe each taste as a pairing of two of the five elements. Sweet is earth and water; pungent is fire and air; bitter is air and space. It links taste back to our earlier post on the five elements.
Taste is how food becomes advice. Our guide describes diet advice in terms of the six tastes, meal timing and what suits a person and a season. Taste is the vocabulary that advice is written in.

Eight factors, read first. Before any rule, the Charaka Samhita names eight factors that decide whether a food suits someone. The same food can be right in one situation and wrong in another.
Nature, preparation, combination: Prakriti, the nature of the food; Karana, how it is prepared; Samyoga, what it is combined with; Rashi, how much is eaten.
Place, time, manner, person: Desha, the place and climate; Kala, the time and season; Upayoga samstha, the rules of eating; Upabhokta, the person who eats.

No food is simply good. Under this reading there are no universal superfoods. Whether a food suits you depends on how it is made, what it meets, how much, where, when, and who you are. The Point: Suitability, not virtue.
Education, not a plan. Eight factors cannot be read from a caption. A vaidya can read them with you, and your doctor's dietary advice for any condition comes first.

A set of rules for the meal. The Charaka Samhita gives a short list of rules for how to eat. Most diets argue about ingredients. This list is almost entirely about manner, timing and attention. Ahara Vidhi: Ahara, food. Vidhi, the method.

Warm, unctuous, enough. The first rules describe the meal: warm, with some fat, in the right quantity, and only after the last meal has digested. warm, a little unctuous, in proper quantity, after digestion.
Not too fast, not too slow. The next rules describe how to sit and eat. not too fast, not too slow, in a pleasant place, not talking or laughing, with attention.
Eat with yourself in mind. The list ends by asking the eater to consider their own body: what suits them, how much, and when. It is the same idea as Prakriti, applied to one plate.
Rules, not a cure. These are the tradition's rules for eating well. We will not claim they treat any disease. Anyone with a medical diet should follow it first, and ask how these fit around it.

Some pairings, the texts say, do not suit. The Charaka Samhita describes viruddha ahara: foods that are unsuitable together, or in a certain quantity, preparation, place or time. It is the combination factor from our last post, in detail. Viruddha: Viruddha: opposed, or incompatible.

Incompatible by more than pairing. The texts describe incompatibility of many kinds, not just two foods together. combination, quantity, preparation, place, time, season, your digestion, your constitution.
Three that come up often: Milk and fish, a combination the texts caution against; Honey and ghee, in equal quantity; Heated honey, a preparation the texts caution against.

It fits the whole framework. If a food's effect depends on its preparation, quantity, season and the person eating it, then incompatibility follows naturally. Viruddha ahara is the framework's logic, not a separate rule.
Not a list of poisons. These are classical cautions. We will not claim that any combination on them causes a specific disease. Modern evidence on most of them is thin, and we say so plainly.

alt: Cover: Still a fat. Where tradition and nutrition agree.

Myth: “The texts say ghee is good, so eat plenty.” What the texts say: The same texts ask for food in proper quantity and say incompatibility can come from quantity alone. Valued is not the same as unlimited.

Myth: “Ghee has no downside.” What the texts say: Ghee is mostly saturated fat. Nutrition guidance generally asks people to keep saturated fat moderate, especially with heart disease or high cholesterol.

Myth: “Any ghee labelled Ayurvedic is medicine.” What the texts say: Medicated ghee preparations contain herbs and should be prescribed, not self chosen. Quality varies by maker, so buy from reputable manufacturers.

Enough, not more. Tradition and modern nutrition land in the same place: a little ghee in a balanced diet, not ghee as a treatment. The quantity is the whole conversation. The Pattern: A spoon, not a jar.
Education, not a plan. If you have heart disease, high cholesterol, diabetes or a weight target, how much ghee suits you is a question for your doctor, not a caption.

Four fats, and one comes first. The Charaka Samhita's chapter on unctuous substances names four: ghee, oil, animal fat and marrow. Among them, it ranks ghee first. Sneha: The classical word for oils and fats.

It carries what it is cooked with. The texts describe ghee as taking on the properties of what it is processed with, without losing its own. That is why so many classical medicines are prepared in ghee: it is a carrier.
A kitchen staple, and a vehicle. Ghee appears in food, in medicine and in ritual. cooking, medicated ghee, oleation before cleansing, lamps, festivals.

A little, with the meal. Traditional teaching links a moderate amount of ghee with good digestion. The rules of eating in our last post say the same in general terms: a little unctuousness, in proper quantity.
Not a superfood. We will not claim ghee treats any disease or that more is better. The texts value it, and they also insist on the right quantity. We report both halves.

Rice, dal, a little ghee. Khichdi is rice and split dal cooked together until soft, usually with a little ghee and mild spice. It is one of the most familiar meals in India, and one of the lightest. In One Line: Soft, warm, simple, and easy to digest.
Easy on Agni. Everything about khichdi makes it easy to digest: it is warm, soft, cooked for a long time and simply spiced. That fits the tradition's constant concern with protecting digestion.

After illness, after cleansing. Traditionally khichdi is a meal for recovery, and the diet that follows cleansing therapies moves gradually from thin gruels to fuller meals. Soft rice and dal preparations sit on that path.

Not a cure in a bowl. Khichdi is a light, familiar meal. We will not claim it heals any illness or detoxes anything. When you are unwell, it is gentle food, and an illness still needs its own care.
